title: White Rooms and Cold Water: the Glasgow Style, the Practice That Failed, and the Painter of Roussillon
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Glasgow, birth in Parson Street
stops.date_confidence: attested; full date given by Wikipedia
stops.campa: In a tenement at 70 Parson Street, in the Townhead district north of the cathedral, the fourth of eleven children is born to a police superintendent and his wife. They name him Charles Rennie Mackintosh. Twenty-seven years later a board school will rise on this same street, built to his own drawings. For now it is a working street in a working city, soot on the stone, the Clyde yards going through the night a mile to the south, and eleven children coming up in the one tenement household.
suggested_refs: 70 Parson Street, Townhead, the birthplace tenement; Martyrs' Public School, built later on the same street

stops.name: Glasgow, Allan Glen's Institution
stops.date_confidence: attested for the school, approximate for the year; the pool gives 1880-1883 without a register reference, and month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: He is sent to Allan Glen's Institution, a Glasgow school weighted toward drawing, mathematics and the practical trades rather than the classics. It is where the technical bent of his hand is first trained, and where a boy out of Townhead can learn to set out an elevation without anyone asking after his father's rank. The father intends him for the ministry. The son intends architecture, and the argument ends in an apprenticeship rather than a place at divinity school. Who else spoke in that quarrel, and how long it ran, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: Allan Glen's Institution, Glasgow, a technical school for the sons of tradesmen

stops.name: Glasgow, articled to John Hutchison
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day are placeholders, and the office address is unrecorded, so the pin is a city-centre placeholder
stops.campa: At sixteen he is articled to the architect John Hutchison, whose office stands somewhere among the commercial streets of the city centre. He learns the trade the way it was then learned: tracing another man's elevations through the working day, walking out to sites, ruling lines to a set width. The apprenticeship fills the daylight hours and the evenings he gives to something else entirely. Half the reference books that carry the name spell it Hutchinson, with an n that does not belong in it. The articles run five years.
suggested_refs: The practice of John Hutchison, architect, Glasgow, where Mackintosh served his articles

stops.name: Glasgow, evening classes on Sauchiehall Street
stops.date_confidence: start year not recorded anywhere reached; the classes run through the later 1880s alongside the apprenticeship, and 1885-01-01 is a placeholder inside that span
stops.campa: The Glasgow School of Art is still on Sauchiehall Street, in hired rooms above shops, when he enrols in the evening classes and begins collecting prizes. Its director, Francis Newbery, takes the applied arts seriously and does not much care whether a student arrives from a drawing office or a shipyard; the teaching runs under the long shadow of John Ruskin, who had taught a generation that ornament must be made by the hand that thought of it. Here Mackintosh meets Margaret and Frances Macdonald and Herbert MacNair. The four of them will be called the Glasgow Four.
suggested_refs: The old Glasgow School of Art rooms on Sauchiehall Street, before the Garnethill building
John Ruskin on honest ornament, the theory the school taught under

stops.name: Glasgow, draughtsman at Honeyman and Keppie
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day are placeholders, and the office address is a reconstruction
stops.campa: He leaves Hutchison for Honeyman and Keppie and joins as a draughtsman. John Honeyman is an established Gothic revivalist near the end of his working life; John Keppie is the younger man who brings in the business and keeps the accounts. Nearly every building Mackintosh will be remembered for is drawn inside this office and issued under the firm's name rather than his own. Twelve years pass before his own name goes up on the door, and the best of the work is behind him by then. He is twenty-one.
suggested_refs: The office of Honeyman and Keppie, Glasgow, inside which almost the whole built oeuvre was drawn

stops.name: Naples, the studentship lands in Italy
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the itinerary is assembled from surviving sketchbooks rather than from letters, and the month is a placeholder inside the travelling season
stops.campa: The Alexander Thomson Travelling Studentship, endowed in memory of the Glasgow architect they called Greek Thomson, pays for Italy. He lands at Naples and begins working north with a sketchbook under his arm. What his training has shown him only as engraved plates in a library he now takes with his own eye: the orders themselves, and the way a cornice cuts against a hot sky. The route is reconstructed afterwards from the pages he filled. No letters home survive to check it against.
suggested_refs: The Mackintosh Italian sketchbooks of 1891, the sole evidence for the route
sources: Alan Crawford, 'Charles Rennie Mackintosh' (general biography, not consulted directly in this pass)

stops.name: Siena, the striped cathedral and the Campo
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from sketchbook attribution; month a placeholder
stops.campa: In Siena he draws the cathedral, its black and white courses of marble banded across the wall like woven cloth, and the brick shell of the Campo sloping down to its drain. He is twenty-three and travelling on other men's money for the first time in his life. What he takes from the city is not classical proportion but pattern: how a flat surface holds the eye by repetition, by a line kept exact along its whole length. The white rooms he will build in Glasgow have no marble in them anywhere. They have the banding.
suggested_refs: Siena cathedral and the Piazza del Campo, drawn in the 1891 sketchbooks
sources: Alan Crawford, 'Charles Rennie Mackintosh' (general biography, not consulted directly in this pass)

stops.name: Ravenna, the mosaics of San Vitale
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from sketchbook attribution; month a placeholder
stops.campa: At San Vitale he stands under Byzantine mosaic set close enough to read, gold tesserae laid slightly out of plane so that the light will not lie flat on them. Biographers connect this room to the flattened, jewelled surfaces of his later decorative work, to the inset glass and beaten metal that will glitter in a Sauchiehall Street tea room thirty years on. The connection is theirs, drawn backward from the finished work. Mackintosh left no note in Ravenna saying what he thought he was learning.
suggested_refs: The apse mosaics of San Vitale, Ravenna, cited by biographers as a source for the later decorative surfaces
sources: Alan Crawford, 'Charles Rennie Mackintosh' (general biography, not consulted directly in this pass)

stops.name: Venice, the end of the tour
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from sketchbook attribution; the day is a placeholder and the return date is unrecorded
stops.campa: He sketches in Venice at the end of the tour, water standing at the foot of every wall, then turns north and home. Three months of Italy close behind him and he goes back to the drawing boards at Honeyman and Keppie to draft other men's designs at a draughtsman's wage. What he took out of the journey surfaces slowly, in stencil and glass and the proportion of a stair tower. The Italian pages go into a portfolio and the portfolio into a cupboard. He is in Glasgow again before the autumn.
suggested_refs: The 1891 Venetian sheets, last of the studentship drawings
sources: Alan Crawford, 'Charles Rennie Mackintosh' (general biography, not consulted directly in this pass)

stops.name: Dumbreck, the interiors at Craigie Hall
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: At Craigie Hall in Dumbreck he remodels interiors for a client of John Honeyman's. The commission is small and the credit belongs to the firm; he is twenty-five and signing nothing. The house stands among villas raised on Clyde money, in a district where a young draughtsman's reputation is made quietly and by word of mouth. The decorative hand is unmistakably his, and anyone who later learns to recognise it can find it here first: an organ case, a doorway, carved detail worked out at full size and handed to the joiners.
suggested_refs: Craigie Hall, 6 Rowan Road, Dumbreck, and its Mackintosh organ case and carved detail

stops.name: Glasgow, rooms for the Art Club in Bath Street
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day are placeholders, and the work runs alongside Craigie Hall in the same year
stops.campa: He redesigns rooms for the Glasgow Art Club in Bath Street, work running alongside the Craigie Hall interiors and part of the same early run of commissions. The Art Club is where the city's painters and architects eat and argue, so the rooms are seen by exactly the men whose opinion decides what a young designer is given next. His name appears on none of it. Honeyman and Keppie is the name on the account. He has been paid by the week since 1889 and is paid by the week still.
suggested_refs: The Glasgow Art Club rooms, Bath Street, remodelled 1893

stops.name: Glasgow, the Herald tower off Mitchell Lane
stops.date_confidence: attested to the span 1893-1895; the single date is a placeholder inside it
stops.campa: For the Glasgow Herald the firm builds a warehouse and offices off Buchanan Street with a water tower at the corner, and the tower is his: a tall shaft carrying a tank against fire, given a crown of stone and small deep windows that owe as much to Scots tower houses as to any revival style. A century later the building is renamed The Lighthouse and handed over to a design museum. The credit at the time goes to Honeyman and Keppie, and he writes privately of hoping one day to claim his own work as his own.
suggested_refs: The Glasgow Herald building, Mitchell Lane, now The Lighthouse, Scotland's centre for design and architecture

stops.name: Townhead, Martyrs' Public School on Parson Street
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the 1895-1898 span was not independently verifiable, so the tag is held at [R] and the date is the span's start
stops.campa: The school board wants a building on Parson Street and the commission comes to the firm; Mackintosh draws it. He is designing on the street he was born in, for the children of the tenements he grew up among. What the art school will do later at full strength is tried out here first, on a board school budget. The roof over the stair is carried on exposed timber brackets and the classrooms take their light from high on the wall, the structure left showing where a duller architect would have plastered it out of sight.
suggested_refs: Martyrs' Public School, Parson Street, Townhead, standing on Mackintosh's own birth street
sources: General survey of Mackintosh buildings; dates not independently confirmed

stops.name: Glasgow, the first tea rooms for Catherine Cranston
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: Catherine Cranston is building a chain of tea rooms in a city arguing hard about drink, and she hires him to decorate walls at her Buchanan Street premises. It is the beginning of a working relationship that runs twenty years and gives him more built work than any other client of his life. She wants rooms that are respectable, cheap to sit in, and unlike anything else in Glasgow. He gives her stencilled figures the full height of the wall, elongated women standing in thickets of stem and rose.
suggested_refs: The Buchanan Street tea rooms of Catherine Cranston, first of the Mackintosh commissions for her

stops.name: Maryhill, the first service at Queen's Cross Church
stops.date_confidence: attested; memorial stone laid 23 June 1898, first service 10 September 1899
stops.campa: The memorial stone goes down in June 1898 and the first service is held on the tenth of September the following year, in the only church of his design that is ever built. It stands on a corner in Maryhill: a squat tower, a traceried east window remembering Gothic without copying it, and inside, timber roof trusses tied with exposed steel like the framing of a ship. He enters a cathedral competition a few years later and wins nothing. No other congregation ever commissions him.
suggested_refs: Queen's Cross Church, Maryhill, the only Mackintosh church built, now the seat of the Charles Rennie Mackintosh Society

stops.name: Garnethill, the east half of the art school
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1899 for the completion of the first half; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: Newbery pushes the commission for a new art school toward the firm, and the design that wins it is Mackintosh's, drawn by a junior man who has never built anything of this size. William Morris had taught the previous generation that a building should be made by hands that understood it, and here that argument is carried out in Glasgow sandstone by a man of thirty. The east half rises on Renfrew Street between 1897 and 1899: a north wall of enormous studio windows over a plain stone base, ironwork brackets crooked out over the glass to carry the window cleaners' planks.
suggested_refs: The Mackintosh Building, Renfrew Street, east wing 1897-1899
The Arts and Crafts inheritance from William Morris, acknowledged ancestor of the Glasgow Style

stops.name: Glasgow, marriage and the white rooms in Mains Street
stops.date_confidence: attested; full date given for the marriage
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of August 1900 he marries Margaret Macdonald, and they take rooms in Mains Street and strip them bare. Walls white, woodwork white, a stencilled panel of rose and stem run up beside a doorway, furniture made to their own design and set deliberately far apart on empty floors. Visitors describe the rooms as unlike any others in the city, and photographs are taken of them almost at once. From here on the work is hard to divide: her gesso panels go into his interiors, and which of them designed what in a finished room is a question the rooms themselves do not answer.
suggested_refs: 120 Mains Street, later Blythswood Street, the first Mackintosh interior made for themselves

stops.name: Vienna, a room at the eighth Secession exhibition
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1900; the eighth Secession exhibition opens in November, and the couple's travel dates are not established here
stops.campa: A room of Mackintosh furniture is crated to Vienna and set up inside the Secession's eighth exhibition, and the reception is warmer than anything Glasgow has given him. The Viennese are building their own case against historical ornament and find in this Scot a man already living inside the conclusion. For a few years his name will mean more in Austria and Germany than it does at home. Josef Hoffmann and the circle that will make the Wiener Werkstatte stand in the room and take note of the spacing, the whiteness, the refusal to fill.
suggested_refs: The Secession Building, Vienna, and the eighth exhibition of 1900 in which the Glasgow room was shown

stops.name: Glasgow, his name on the door at last
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day are placeholders, and the office address remains a reconstruction
stops.campa: Twelve years after walking in as a draughtsman he is made a partner, and the firm is renamed Honeyman, Keppie and Mackintosh. Honeyman retires. The art school stands half built, the tea rooms are running, the Continental journals are printing his interiors, and he is thirty-three years old with a practice under his own name. The great commissions run from 1895 to 1906 and this year falls in the middle of them. From this office the work will thin, slowly and then completely, across the following twelve years.
suggested_refs: The partnership of Honeyman, Keppie and Mackintosh, formed 1901

stops.name: Glasgow, the portfolio for a house with no site
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the competition; month and day are placeholders. The stop is pinned where the drawings were made, since the competition was for an imaginary house and the Bellahouston site is a 1980s decision
stops.campa: The German magazine Zeitschrift fur Innendekoration announces a competition for a house for an art lover, and he and Margaret draw one: hall, dining room, music room, a long white exterior carrying almost no ornament at all. Thirty-six portfolios come in. Theirs arrives late and short of the required interior perspectives and is disqualified on those grounds, then given a special prize regardless. The house is a set of drawings for a place that does not exist, and Glasgow will build it in Bellahouston Park eighty-eight years later. There is no site and there is no client.
stops.quote: pronounced personal quality, novel and austere form and the uniform configuration of interior and exterior
stops.quote_source: The competition judges on the Mackintosh portfolio, quoted via Graham Roxburgh, Building the Dream (2006), as cited on Wikipedia; Roxburgh's book not consulted directly
suggested_refs: The Haus eines Kunstfreundes portfolio of 1901
House for an Art Lover, built from the drawings in Bellahouston Park, Glasgow, 1989-1996

stops.name: Turin, the Scottish room at the exhibition
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; carried by the general biography and not independently confirmed, with the month a placeholder
stops.campa: He and Margaret design and furnish a Scottish room at the international exhibition of decorative art in Turin, white and sparse among pavilions competing to out-elaborate their neighbours. No foreign audience will take the Glasgow Style this seriously again. Two countries away from home, in halls of gilt and moulded plaster, the room reads as a room out of another century, and the visitors cannot agree which century that is. In the same year he lectures in Glasgow under the title Seemliness and closes with one line.
stops.quote: Art is the Flower - Life is the Green Leaf
stops.quote_source: Charles Rennie Mackintosh, closing line of the lecture Seemliness, Glasgow, 1902, as given on Wikiquote
suggested_refs: The Scottish section at the Esposizione Internazionale d'Arte Decorativa Moderna, Turin, 1902
The lecture Seemliness, Glasgow, 1902
sources: General Mackintosh biography, not independently confirmed

stops.name: Kilmacolm, Windyhill for William Davidson
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the design is placed at 1900-1901 by the general survey, address and coordinates not independently confirmed
stops.campa: For William Davidson he builds a house on high ground at Kilmacolm: roughcast harling pulled over the walls, windows set where they are wanted rather than where symmetry would put them, the roof dragged down low against Renfrewshire weather. It is his first complete country house, and it settles the method he will use again at Helensburgh, which is to design the inside first and let the outside follow from it. There is almost no ornament on the outside at all.
suggested_refs: Windyhill, Kilmacolm, built for William Davidson
sources: General survey of Mackintosh buildings; not independently confirmed

stops.name: Helensburgh, Hill House for Walter Blackie
stops.date_confidence: attested; design begins 1902 and the house is completed 1904, so the single date is the start of the commission
stops.campa: Walter Blackie, a Glasgow publisher, wants a house on the hill above the Clyde at Helensburgh and gets one for five thousand pounds. Mackintosh asks first how the family actually lives, arranges the rooms around the answers, and only afterwards shows an elevation. It is the most complete surviving statement of his domestic architecture, and the Portland cement render on its walls will fail inside a century. Inside, the plaster is white and the timber dark stained, the hall like a wood, the bedroom furniture designed so exactly for its corners that moving it would be vandalism.
stops.quote: Not until we had decided on these inside arrangements did he submit drawings of the elevations.
stops.quote_source: Walter Blackie, client, on Mackintosh's method, quoted on Wikipedia citing a 2018 Dezeen article on Blackie's memoir; the memoir not consulted directly
suggested_refs: Hill House, Helensburgh
The Hill House Box by Carmody Groarke for the National Trust for Scotland, installed 2019 and scheduled to stand until 2028

stops.name: Liverpool, the cathedral competition
stops.date_confidence: contradiction not resolved: the pool dates his entry 1903, but the competition opened in late 1901 and was decided in 1903, so dating the entry to 1903 conflates submission with verdict. 1902 is used as a midpoint placeholder
stops.campa: The competition for a new Anglican cathedral at Liverpool draws a hundred and three entries, and one of them is his. Giles Gilbert Scott, twenty-two years old and barely qualified, wins it. It is the second great competition Mackintosh loses in three years, and the second design of his that will never stand anywhere. The sources disagree about when he entered, since the competition opens late in 1901 and is decided in 1903, and his entry is often dated to the verdict rather than to the drawing. Whether he ever stood on St James's Mount and looked at the ground is not recorded.
suggested_refs: The Liverpool Anglican Cathedral competition of 1901-1903, in which Mackintosh was one of 103 entrants

stops.name: Sauchiehall Street, the Willow Tea Rooms open
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1903 for the opening; the day is a placeholder
stops.campa: At 217 Sauchiehall Street he is given everything for the first time: the front, the back, the furniture, the cutlery, the waitresses' dresses. A four storey building is stripped and remade for Catherine Cranston, its facade white and asymmetrical among red sandstone neighbours, and the Room de Luxe upstairs is fitted with silver painted chairs, leaded mirror glass and a frieze of willow. It opens in October 1903. Hermann Muthesius, writing from Berlin, describes an architect holding out alone against the taste of his own city.
stops.quote: hold up the banner of Beauty in this dense jungle of ugliness
stops.quote_source: Hermann Muthesius on Mackintosh, Dekorative Kunst, 1905, English wording as quoted on Wikipedia; the German original and its translator were not reached
suggested_refs: The Willow Tea Rooms, 217 Sauchiehall Street, and the Room de Luxe; restored and reopened 2018

stops.name: Kingston, Scotland Street School
stops.date_confidence: attested to the span 1903-1906, opened 1906; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: Across the river in Kingston, opposite the tenements that will fill it, he builds a board school with two stair towers glazed from the pavement to the roof, so that the climb to the classroom happens in full daylight. Conical caps sit over them like the turrets of a Scots castle turned to glass, and the two towers are visible from three streets away. It opens in 1906. It works as a school until 1979, by which time the tenements opposite have been cleared and there are no children left within walking distance.
suggested_refs: Scotland Street School, Kingston, Glasgow, now Scotland Street School Museum

stops.name: Hillhead, the house on Southpark Avenue
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the move to 6 Florentine Terrace, later 78 Southpark Avenue; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: They move from Mains Street to a terraced house near the university at Hillhead, and he does to it what he did to the flat: white walls, dark stencil, silvered metal, furniture placed as carefully as sculpture and lit as carefully as sculpture. Sixty years on the terrace is demolished and the interiors are taken out room by room and rebuilt inside a gallery a short walk away, at a different height above the ground. It is the last house the two of them make together in Glasgow.
suggested_refs: The Mackintosh House, reconstructed from 78 Southpark Avenue and opened inside the Hunterian, University of Glasgow, in 1981

stops.name: Garnethill, the library finished
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1909 for the completion of the second half; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: The second half of the art school is finished in 1909, and at its west end he builds the library: a room three storeys deep, hung with a forest of dark posts and beams, lit through oriel windows running nearly the height of the wall. Every surface in it is timber, cut, notched, and left showing. It is the room by which his reputation as an architect is settled. On a May afternoon in 2014 a canister of expanding foam ignites near a hot projector inside it, and the room burns entirely.
suggested_refs: The Mackintosh Library, Glasgow School of Art, completed 1909, destroyed by fire 23 May 2014

stops.name: Glasgow, resignation from the firm
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the resignation; month and day are placeholders, and the decline in profitability is placed vaguely at the early 1910s
stops.campa: The partnership stops paying. Commissions thin through the early 1910s, and in 1913 he resigns from the firm that carries his name and sets up on his own account. Almost nothing comes in. A man of forty-five with the finest building in the city to his credit finds that Glasgow has stopped asking. The reasons offered afterwards, that he was difficult to work with, that he drank, that the fashion had turned against him, are all supplied by people writing long after the fact. Neither partner left an explanation.
stops.quote: There is hope in honest error, none in the icy perfection of the mere stylist.
stops.quote_source: J. D. Sedding, English architect; a line Mackintosh adopted as a personal motto. Wikiquote notes it is frequently misattributed to Mackintosh himself and it is not his sentence
suggested_refs: The dissolution of Honeyman, Keppie and Mackintosh, 1913

stops.name: Walberswick, the flower drawings
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the move; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: They give up Glasgow and go to Walberswick on the Suffolk coast, a fishing village of shingle, marsh and enormous sky, where an architect with no commissions can live cheaply. He puts down the drawing instruments and picks up watercolour, working close to the ground on flower studies: a single stem, its structure set out as exactly as a section through a stair. He is forty-six and out of the profession he trained for. The war begins a few weeks after they arrive.
suggested_refs: The Walberswick flower studies of 1914-1915

stops.name: Walberswick, detained as a spy
stops.date_confidence: widely repeated in the biographical literature and given as attested by one half of the research pool, unconfirmed by the other; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: A village on the North Sea in the first year of the war watches its strangers. Someone reports the Scot who walks the marshes at odd hours with a sketchbook and receives letters in German from Vienna and Munich, and he is detained and questioned as a suspected enemy agent. No charge follows. The correspondence that had once been the proof of his European reputation is now the thing that makes him unwelcome on an English coast. They leave Suffolk.
suggested_refs: The wartime detention at Walberswick, 1915, reported in the biographical literature
sources: Crawford and the general biography; not confirmed in the Walberswick article

stops.name: Chelsea, the studio in Glebe Place
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the year is carried by the general biography, month and day are placeholders, and the house number is disputed
stops.campa: They take a studio in Glebe Place, Chelsea, among painters' houses and the addresses of architects already better known than he is. Voysey and Lutyens have London, and London does not need another. He is forty-seven, with nothing under construction anywhere. He draws a block of studios for the street itself, which is never built, and takes what small design work comes to him. Even the number of the house is uncertain now: some sources say 43A, others 49, and the two cannot both be right.
suggested_refs: Glebe Place, Chelsea, and the unbuilt studio block designed for the street
sources: General Mackintosh biography; address not confirmed

stops.name: Northampton, 78 Derngate remade
stops.date_confidence: attested to the span 1916-1917 for the remodelling; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: Wenman Bassett-Lowke, who manufactures model railway engines in Northampton, buys a narrow Georgian terrace house and hires Mackintosh to remake it. He rebuilds the back, opens the ground floor, and covers the hall in black with a stencilled band of triangles climbing the wall in yellow, grey and blue, chevrons stepping across the stripes of the guest bedroom. It is later called one of the first Art Deco interiors in Britain, a decade before the phrase exists. In 1926 the Bassett-Lowkes leave it for a modernist house in concrete.
suggested_refs: 78 Derngate, Northampton, remodelled for W. J. Bassett-Lowke 1916-1917

stops.name: Chelsea, patterns and book covers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the pool downgrades this from attested because it was not confirmed in the article checked, and the 1920-1923 span is approximate
stops.campa: With no architecture left to design he earns from the Chelsea studio by drawing textile repeats and book bindings, some of them said to be for Blackie and Son of Glasgow, the firm whose director had once given him Hill House. He is in his fifties and nothing of his is being built. The work is anonymous and paid by the piece; most of it cannot now be identified with certainty, the period is thinly documented, and the Blackie attribution rests on very little that can be checked. Who bought the rest of the patterns, and what was made from them, no source reached will say.
suggested_refs: The Chelsea textile designs and book bindings of the early 1920s, largely unattributed
sources: Wikipedia, 'Charles Rennie Mackintosh'; the Blackie attribution not confirmed in the current article

stops.name: Port Vendres, the crossing south
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: Broke, they cross to the French Mediterranean and settle at Port Vendres, a small fishing and naval port where the Pyrenees run down into the sea an hour's walk from the Spanish border. Living is cheap and the light is long. He gives up architecture altogether and paints watercolour full time: the harbour, the fort above it, the rock strata behind the town set down with the precision he once gave to a stair detail. He works standing, in strong sun. The finished sheets go off to London, where no exhibition is ever arranged for them.
suggested_refs: Port Vendres, Roussillon, and the watercolours made there between 1923 and 1927
sources: Charles Rennie Mackintosh Society, Port Vendres page

stops.name: Collioure, the harbour and the fortress
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; carried by the general Roussillon literature, and which sheet belongs to which year is largely guesswork
stops.campa: He walks the coast road to Collioure, where Matisse and Derain had spent a summer twenty years earlier and made the town famous for colour. Mackintosh paints it differently. He is working more steadily now than he has worked at anything since the art school library went up, and his Roussillon watercolours are built the way elevations are built: the fortress and the bell tower drawn out in pencil first and filled in afterwards, the edges kept hard, the sea laid down as one flat plane of blue.
suggested_refs: The Collioure watercolours of the Roussillon period
sources: General Mackintosh biography, Roussillon watercolour period; not independently confirmed

stops.name: Mont-Louis, the citadel in the Cerdagne
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; carried by the general Roussillon literature, month and day placeholders
stops.campa: Inland and high, in the Cerdagne, he paints the fortified town of Mont-Louis: Vauban's walls, a citadel over a valley, snow country in winter. The sheets from this stretch are built over dense pencil underdrawing, almost architectural in their preparation, the paint laid into a structure already fully worked out before any colour touches it. The tour is reconstructed from the paintings themselves, as the Italian tour of 1891 was reconstructed from the sketchbooks. He reaches these places on foot and by local train, carrying paints and a folding stool.
suggested_refs: The Mont-Louis watercolours; Vauban's citadel in the Cerdagne
sources: General Mackintosh biography, Roussillon watercolour period; not independently confirmed

stops.name: Ille-sur-Tet, one of the last French sheets
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; carried by the general Roussillon literature, month and day placeholders
stops.campa: Among the last of the French watercolours is a view of Ille-sur-Tet in the valley of the Tet, stone houses stacked along a slope, rendered in the exact and almost cartographic line he once used for elevations. He is fifty-eight years old. Something in his throat has begun to hurt. He is exhibiting nowhere and selling nothing, and he is better at this than anyone in London has noticed. The sheet is finished, signed and put in the folder with the others.
suggested_refs: The Ille-sur-Tet watercolour, among the last of the French period
sources: General Mackintosh biography, Roussillon watercolour period; not independently confirmed

stops.name: Port Vendres, leaving the harbour
stops.date_confidence: the return to London in 1927 is attested; the scene in the port is a reconstruction and the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: The soreness in his tongue does not go. Through the winter it worsens until he cannot eat properly or make himself understood, and the doctors of a small port can do nothing with it. Friends press him to go back to London where there is treatment. He puts it off, then agrees. He packs the watercolours, four years of them, and leaves the harbour he has painted from every angle it can be painted from. Which month he left, no source reached records.
suggested_refs: The last Port Vendres harbour views, 1926-1927
sources: General Mackintosh biography; the scene not independently confirmed

stops.name: Westminster Hospital, the diagnosis
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: In London the diagnosis is cancer of the tongue. He is treated at Westminster Hospital with surgery and with radium, and the surgery takes his voice down to a whisper he never gets back. The hospital stands a few streets from the Abbey, in a city he had come to twelve years before hoping for work and had been given almost none. Nobody in England is writing about him. He is fifty-nine years old and has been out of practice for fourteen years. Roughly a dozen buildings anywhere carry his hand.
suggested_refs: Westminster Hospital, London, where Mackintosh was treated for tongue cancer in 1927

stops.name: Hampstead, convalescence on Willow Road
stops.date_confidence: attested to the span 1927-1928; the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: He convalesces in Hampstead as the guest of the painter Randolph Schwabe and his wife Birdie, on Willow Road below the Heath. He cannot work. The voice is gone, the strength going, and the days pass in a borrowed room with a window on a north London street. It is the last address at which he is anything other than a patient. The visitors are few, and the ones who come are painters rather than architects, so that what talk there is runs on pictures rather than on buildings. He stays in the house on Willow Road through the winter of 1927.
suggested_refs: The Schwabe household on Willow Road, Hampstead, where Mackintosh convalesced

stops.name: Bayswater, death at 26 Porchester Square
stops.date_confidence: attested; full date and age given
stops.campa: His friend Desmond Chapman-Huston finds them rooms at 12 Porchester Square in Bayswater, and when the illness turns he is moved to a nursing home at number 26 on the same square. The nearest building of his own is sixty miles away, a terrace house in Northampton with a black hall. The practice had been finished for fifteen years and the art school library was standing intact in Glasgow. He dies there on the tenth of December 1928, aged sixty, thirteen months after leaving Port Vendres.
suggested_refs: 12 and 26 Porchester Square, Bayswater; the nursing home in which Mackintosh died

stops.name: Golders Green, the cremation
stops.date_confidence: attested; cremated the day after his death
stops.campa: He is cremated on the eleventh of December at Golders Green in north London, twenty-four hours after his death, in a suburb of a city that never gave him a building. What survives of him is a set of rooms in Glasgow, a house at Helensburgh, a school in Kingston, a church in Maryhill and a remade terrace house in Northampton, together with several hundred sheets of paper, and for the next thirty years almost nobody goes looking for any of it. There is no grave and there will be none.
suggested_refs: Golders Green Crematorium, 62 Hoop Lane, London NW11

stops.name: Port Vendres, the ashes on the water
stops.date_confidence: date unrecorded; no source reached gives one, and 1929-01-01 is an explicit placeholder after the December 1928 cremation
stops.campa: His ashes are carried back to the Mediterranean and scattered off Port Vendres, from rocks he had stood on and painted, which is what he had asked for. No source records the day it was done. Sixty years after his death Glasgow builds the house he and Margaret drew for a German magazine, and puts it in a park at Bellahouston. Then the art school burns, in 2014 and again in 2018. The shell left standing after the second fire is due to reopen in 2030.
